works.abstract: The Papahānaumokuākea Marine Debris Project (PMDP) is a nonprofit organization that conducts operations to locate and remove marine debris from coral reef ecosystems within the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument (PMNM). Currently, diver fatigue during scouting operations from free swimming in open water limits the range and efficiency of these missions. To address this challenge, this project developed a compact DPV designed to assist divers in surface scouting and debris recovery operations. The system was required to satisfy several operational and safety requirements, including propelling a 70 kg diver at a minimum speed of 2.7 km/hr, providing at least 30 minutes of continuous runtime, and ensuring diver safety throughout operation of the DPV. The final prototype consists of a surface-operating DPV incorporating dual T500 thrusters, electronic components housed within a sealed waterproof enclosure, and epoxy-coated 3D printed structural components. Operation of the DPV is intentionally straightforward: the user first installs the batteries, then seals the enclosure, and can finally activate propulsion using two integrated handle-mounted control buttons. Experimental testing demonstrated that the system can propel a diver at an average speed of 4.3 km/hr, exceeding the required propulsion speed of 2.7 km/hr. Runtime testing confirmed 40 minutes of continuous operation without exhausting the battery capacity, with an estimated total runtime of approximately 1 hour and 40 minutes. Waterproofing tests showed no water ingress after two hours of submersion, confirming the safety and reliability of the electrical system. These results demonstrate that the prototype satisfies the primary engineering requirements and provides a practical propulsion solution to support PMDP’s marine debris removal operations.
works.title: Diver Propulsion Vehicle for Net Recovery in Shallow Reefs

works.abstract: The Papahānaumokuākea Marine Debris Project (PMDP) conducts expeditions to the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands to remove abandoned fishing nets called ghost nets, which pose a severe threat to coral reef ecosystems and marine wildlife. Current retrieval methods require divers to search for ghost nets, then manually cut those nets into smaller pieces and transport them individually to the surface. This process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and physically demanding. Team Nothing but Net designed the Net Elevator, an inflatable Zodiac speedboat with its floor removed, fitted with a rigid aluminum frame and four manually operated winches, to transport up to 5,000 lbs of ghost nets as a single contained mass from the site of collection to the mothership. The device exploits the near-neutral buoyancy of ghost nets, transitioning through three operating mechanisms: lift initiation, in which the winches raise the net load off the seabed toward the surface; equilibrium carrying, in which the net mass is suspended partially above and partially below the waterline, with the ratio determined by the available buoyancy of the raft and the density and mass of the net clump; and towing, in which the unpowered raft is pulled alongside an operating Zodiac to transport the load to the mothership. This mothership is a large ship that houses all of the crew, Zodiacs, and equipment, and it acts as the central hub on these missions. This approach mobilizes loads far exceeding the raft's standalone capacity. The design was validated through three experiments: a PVC patch peel test, an operational test conducted at Shoreline Lake, and a static load test reaching 2,000 lbs. Results confirmed that the frame sustained no permanent deformation under load, the PVC patch connection withstood anticipated operational forces, and the full operation sequence was successfully executed on the water. Based on these results and supporting FEA analysis, the team is confident the design can be scaled to a full-sized PMDP Zodiac and meet the 5,000 lb lifting requirement.
works.title: Net Elevator: Lifting Apparatus for PMDP Ghost Nets
